nodes.line: Long day. Say what you came to say.

This is going to sound small. I start at half six and for a month the Canterbury back lane has had somebody in it who is not waiting for bread. Everyone I have told has looked at me the way you are now. Do not make a scene about it.

I have written it down twice and lost it twice. A light on that lane costs Canterbury $35 and the landlord has said no twice, so we are doing it ourselves. This is the third time I have had this conversation. Ask for me by name at the counter.
Alright. I am listening properly this time.

choices.text: half six at Canterbury — that's done.
The Lane Light, Canterbury — that's done.

nodes.line: Suit yourself. The offer does not go anywhere.
I know that look. Everyone wants something today.

Do not laugh. The flour for Canterbury comes off a truck at half six and last the Sunday after payday the truck came and the flour did not. It started small, the way these things do. Come back and tell me straight.

It is the sort of thing you notice or you do not. The Canterbury loading zone has had a car in it at half six every morning this week and the driver waits in it, which makes it worse. It is the not knowing that has got me, honestly. Do that and we're square.
Say it plain and I will pay you plain.

choices.text: The Loading Zone, Canterbury — that's done.

nodes.line: No dramas. Come back when you are bored.

npcs.name: Cleo, front of house at Canterbury

nodes.line: Give me a second. Right. Go.

Two people have already said no. Somebody two doors down from Canterbury put up a sign on the Sunday after payday that says the same six words as ours, in the same order. There is probably a simple explanation and I would love to hear it. I will owe you one, and I pay those.

Someone has to, and it may as well be you. This business was at Hurlstone Park before it was at Canterbury, and there is a woman there who still has the original book. You will see what I mean the second you get there. Do not let them talk you into anything.
I had a feeling. Go on.

choices.text: The Sourdough Sign, Canterbury — that's done.
The Old Site, Canterbury — that's done.

nodes.line: Right you are. Mind the step.
You are not from around the corner, are you.

This is going to sound small. Council has been saying the Pennant Hills pool is at end of life since grand final week and the crack they keep pointing at is not in the shell. Everyone I have told has looked at me the way you are now. Do not make a scene about it.

I have written it down twice and lost it twice. We are running a stall for Pennant Hills on grand final week and a stall needs $33 of gear that nobody has volunteered to pay for. This is the third time I have had this conversation. Ask for me by name at the counter.
Take a breath. Then say the whole thing.

choices.text: The Pennant Hills Pool — that's done.
The Petition Stall, Pennant Hills — that's done.

nodes.line: No dramas. Come back when you are bored.

npcs.name: Mercer, swim coach at Pennant Hills

nodes.line: Half of this suburb has walked past already. Not one stopped.
Do not laugh. I coach 19 kids at Pennant Hills at half six and three of them have stopped coming without anybody ringing me. It started small, the way these things do. Come back and tell me straight.

It is the sort of thing you notice or you do not. A group has been coming over the Pennant Hills fence after close and swimming in the dark, which is how Pennant Hills loses its pool. It is the not knowing that has got me, honestly. Do that and we're square.
Go on then. What did you find.

choices.text: The Deep End, Pennant Hills — that's done.

nodes.line: Right you are. Mind the step.

npcs.name: Jaya, kiosk operator at Pennant Hills

nodes.line: Whatever it is, I have had worse this week.

Two people have already said no. The kiosk at Pennant Hills has a bucket of odd keys in it and a freezer that has been running warm since grand final week. There is probably a simple explanation and I would love to hear it. I will owe you one, and I pay those.

Someone has to, and it may as well be you. They want everyone from Pennant Hills to drive to the new centre at Beecroft, so somebody should go and see whether it is any good. You will see what I mean the second you get there. Do not let them talk you into anything.
You came back. That already puts you ahead.

choices.text: The Kiosk Freezer, Pennant Hills — that's done.
The Aquatic Centre, Pennant Hills — that's done.

nodes.line: Fair enough. You know where I am.

npcs.name: Sian, taxi driver at Edmondson Park

nodes.line: Sit down if you like. Nobody else is using it.

This is going to sound small. The rank outside Edmondson Park used to hold nine cars and since a public holiday nobody remembered it holds four, and nobody will say who moved the line. Everyone I have told has looked at me the way you are now. Do not make a scene about it.

I have written it down twice and lost it twice. Since the rank at Edmondson Park shrank I am $43 a week down, and the association wants that number from somebody who can prove it. This is the third time I have had this conversation. Ask for me by name at the counter.
Right. Tell me and do not soften it.

choices.text: The Edmondson Park Rank — that's done.
Lost Fares, Edmondson Park — that's done.

nodes.line: Right you are. Mind the step.

npcs.name: Fiona, rank marshal at Edmondson Park

nodes.line: You will have to speak up, the trains are in.

Do not laugh. Cars that have never sat in the Edmondson Park queue turn up at the second express and take the front of it, and the drivers who waited say nothing. It started small, the way these things do. Come back and tell me straight.

It is the sort of thing you notice or you do not. When the last train into Edmondson Park is late, 20 people come out at once and I have to have cars there before they do. It is the not knowing that has got me, honestly. Do that and we're square.
I have been thinking about it all day. Out with it.

choices.text: Queue Jumpers, Edmondson Park — that's done.
The Late Train, Edmondson Park — that's done.

nodes.line: Fair enough. You know where I am.

npcs.name: Jia, hotel doorman at Edmondson Park

nodes.line: I have got about four minutes before I am needed.

Two people have already said no. I have stood on this door near Edmondson Park for 20 years and since a public holiday nobody remembered somebody has been sending my guests to a different rank. There is probably a simple explanation and I would love to hear it. I will owe you one, and I pay those.

Someone has to, and it may as well be you. The plates working the Edmondson Park rank are dispatched from a depot at Macquarie Fields, and the man who runs it has never met a driver he liked. You will see what I mean the second you get there. Do not let them talk you into anything.
Well? I can read your face from here.

choices.text: The Door, Edmondson Park — that's done.
The Depot, Edmondson Park — that's done.

nodes.line: Suit yourself. The offer does not go anywhere.
